subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Find the circumcentre of triangle whose vertices are (1,3), (0,−2), (−3,1).

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — say what property defines the circumcentre, and how many equations you need.

steps.label: Set up the equal-distance condition
steps.margin_note: First mark. The circumcentre is the one point equally far from all three vertices, so the whole answer is the single line SA = SB = SC turned into algebra.
steps.memory_tip: The circumcentre is the one point equally far from all three vertices: SA = SB = SC turned into algebra.

recall.must_convey: That S(x, y) is taken as the circumcentre and SA = SB = SC is written down.

the circumcentre is equidistant from all three vertices

steps.why: The circumcentre is DEFINED by being equidistant from the vertices, so that definition is the equation. Two of the three equalities are enough to pin one point.
common_mistakes: Confusing the circumcentre with the centroid and averaging the coordinates.
Using only one equality, which leaves a whole line of possible points.

steps.label: Draw the triangle
steps.margin_note: Worth no mark but worth drawing. The dashed lines are perpendicular BISECTORS — they cut each side in half at a right angle, which is what the equal-distance condition means geometrically.
steps.memory_tip: The dashed lines are perpendicular BISECTORS — that is what equal distances mean geometrically.

recall.must_convey: That a triangle is sketched with two perpendicular bisectors meeting at S. Naming the drawing is full credit — it cannot be spoken.
accept: draw the triangle and the perpendicular bisectors meeting at S
sketch triangle A B C with the bisectors of two sides
make a diagram showing the circumcentre
triangle geesi perpendicular bisectors mark cheyyali
draw the triangle with its perpendicular bisectors

steps.why: The circumcentre is equally far from all three vertices, and the set of points equally far from two vertices IS the perpendicular bisector of the side joining them.
common_mistakes: Drawing altitudes, which give the orthocentre instead.
Drawing medians, which give the centroid.

steps.label: First equation from SA = SB
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Square both sides at once — the square roots vanish and, better, the x² and y² terms cancel across the equals sign, so a SECOND-degree statement collapses to a FIRST-degree line. That collapse is the whole reason this method works.
steps.memory_tip: Square both sides: the x² and y² terms CANCEL, so a second-degree statement collapses to a line.
lines: Squaring on both sides, we get

recall.must_convey: That squaring SA = SB and cancelling the squared terms gives the first linear equation.
accept: square both sides of S A equals S B and the x squared and y squared cancel leaving a straight line
take S A equal to S B, square, and simplify to a linear equation
the second degree terms cancel so we get equation one
S A equals S B square chesthe x square y square cancel avuthaayi
this gives the first equation

steps.why: Both sides carry x² + y², so subtracting removes them. What survives is the perpendicular bisector of AB — a line, which is far easier to work with than a circle.
common_mistakes: Squaring only one side of the equality.
Forgetting to cancel and carrying x² terms into the next step.

steps.label: Second equation from SB = SC
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Exactly the same move on a different pair. Use SB = SC rather than SA = SC — the arithmetic reuses the B expansion already written above.
steps.memory_tip: Use SB = SC rather than SA = SC — it reuses the B expansion already written.

recall.must_convey: That squaring SB = SC and cancelling gives the second linear equation.

square S B equals S C and cancel the squared terms

steps.why: Two perpendicular bisectors meet at exactly one point, so two equations are enough — the third equality carries no new information.
common_mistakes: Using SA = SC and redoing the A expansion for no benefit.
Sign slip when expanding a bracket with a negative coordinate.

steps.label: Solve the pair
steps.margin_note: The last three marks. Two linear equations in two unknowns — solve them any way you like; here subtracting (2) from (1) removes x in one step. The answer is a single point.
steps.memory_tip: Two linear equations, two unknowns, one point.
lines: Step-3: Solving (1) and (2), we get S;

recall.must_convey: That solving the two equations gives ∴ Circumcentre S(x, y) = (−1/3, 2/3).
accept: solve the two equations together to get the circumcentre
subtract equation two from equation one to remove x
solving the pair gives the point

steps.why: The circumcentre can sit outside the triangle when the triangle is obtuse, so an answer far from the vertices is not automatically wrong.
common_mistakes: Subtracting the two equations the wrong way round, so the sign of y comes out reversed.
Writing the coordinates the wrong way round.

insider_note: Square both sides straight away — the x² and y² terms cancel every time, so no root ever survives. Two linear equations are left, and subtracting them here removes x in a single step.
